content_config.text: 1. Overview — The Foot as a Functional Unit

content_config.body:
The foot contains 26 bones, 33 joints and more than 100 ligaments, moved by 12 extrinsic and 20 intrinsic muscles. That complexity exists to solve one problem: the foot must be a flexible shock absorber at heel strike and a rigid lever at push-off — twice per step, on every step.

The ankle above it carries the highest loads per unit of contact area in the body, on a small wedge-shaped bone with no muscle attached to it at all. It is a mortise — a carpenter’s joint — and works only while that mortise stays intact.

rows: Accepts load; the subtalar joint converts leg rotation into foot inversion and eversion
The arch; locks and unlocks to switch the foot between flexible and rigid

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
The single organising idea of the foot. At heel strike the subtalar joint pronates, the midtarsal joint unlocks, and the foot becomes a mobile adapter that absorbs shock and conforms to the ground. Through midstance into push-off the subtalar joint supinates, the midtarsal joint locks, the windlass tightens, and the same foot becomes a rigid lever for propulsion.

Nearly every foot disorder you will treat is a failure of one half of that cycle: a foot that will not unlock (cavus, rigid, coalition) or a foot that will not re-lock (planus, posterior tibial dysfunction, hallux rigidus). Ask which one it is before anything else.
1.2 The joints, and what each contributes

rows: Tibial plafond + both malleoli ↔ talar trochlea
A hinge, but an oblique one — so motion is never purely sagittal
The joint that adapts the foot to uneven ground
Minimal — a few degrees of widening and rotation
A fibrous joint, not synovial. It holds the mortise together
Locks and unlocks under subtalar control
The hinge between hindfoot and midfoot
A rigid keystone arch; injuries here are frequently missed
The hallux MTP needs ~65° for normal gait

content_config.body: • Functionally the midtarsal (Chopart) joint — talonavicular plus calcaneocuboid — must be included too, because it locks and unlocks under subtalar control and determines whether the foot is a flexible shock absorber or a rigid lever.

• The tibial plafond forms the roof, the medial malleolus the short medial wall, and the lateral malleolus the long lateral wall.
  • The lateral malleolus extends about 1 cm further distally and lies more posteriorly than the medial. It is therefore a deeper wall on the lateral side.
  • Consequence: the bony architecture blocks eversion more effectively than inversion. Combined with a weaker lateral ligament complex, this is why inversion sprains vastly outnumber eversion sprains.

content_config.text: 1.3.1 The wedge — the single most useful fact about the ankle

content_config.body:
• The talar trochlea is wider anteriorly than posteriorly, by roughly 2–3 mm.
  • In dorsiflexion, the wide anterior part is driven into the mortise. The joint is close-packed: congruent, tight and maximally stable.
  • In plantarflexion, the narrow posterior part sits in the mortise. The joint is loose-packed: relatively lax and unstable.

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
This wedge explains most of ankle pathology.

Why sprains happen in plantarflexion. Landing, stepping off a kerb or coming down from a jump all load the ankle in plantarflexion, where the joint is loose and the ATFL is the taut structure. That is the mechanism of the classic inversion sprain.

Why dorsiflexion range is protective. A stiff ankle that cannot dorsiflex spends more of its stance phase in the unstable plantarflexed position — which is why restoring dorsiflexion range is the first goal after a sprain, and why limited dorsiflexion predicts re-injury.

Why the syndesmosis must give. Because the talus is wider anteriorly, the mortise must widen slightly in dorsiflexion — the fibula moves laterally about 1 mm and rotates externally. A syndesmosis that is fixed too tightly at surgery blocks dorsiflexion.

Why testing position matters. Perform the anterior drawer test in slight plantarflexion to unlock the joint; test dorsiflexion range with the knee both extended and flexed (the Silfverskiöld test) to separate gastrocnemius tightness from a true joint restriction.

rows: A few degrees of supination and pronation
Adapts the forefoot to the ground

content_config.body:
• Note the inversion-to-eversion ratio of roughly 2:1 to 3:1 — another reason inversion injuries predominate.
  • Stairs, squatting and rising from a chair demand considerably more dorsiflexion than level walking — up to 20–30°.

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
Ten degrees of dorsiflexion is the number to remember. Below that, the body must compensate somewhere: early heel rise, midfoot collapse and pronation (the foot borrows the range from the midtarsal joint), knee hyperextension, or an out-toed gait.

This makes limited dorsiflexion a genuine upstream cause of plantar fasciitis, Achilles tendinopathy, posterior tibial dysfunction, metatarsalgia and knee pain. Measure it in every lower limb assessment, and use the Silfverskiöld test: if dorsiflexion improves markedly with the knee flexed, the restriction is gastrocnemius (which crosses the knee); if it does not, the restriction is soleus or the joint itself.

content_config.body:
• The talocrural joint transmits roughly 5 × body weight in walking and up to 13 × body weight in running.
  • It does this across a small contact area — much smaller than the hip or knee.
  • But primary ankle osteoarthritis is rare, unlike at the hip and knee. Around 70–80% of ankle arthritis is post-traumatic.

content_config.text: 1.5.1 How load is shared across the foot

content_config.body:
• In quiet standing, roughly 50% of load passes through the heel and 50% through the forefoot.
  • Across the forefoot, the first ray carries about twice the load of each lesser ray — roughly a 2:1:1:1:1 distribution.
  • At push-off the forefoot carries essentially all of the body weight, concentrated under the first and second metatarsal heads.
  • Clinical consequence: anything that unloads the first ray — hallux rigidus, a hypermobile first ray, a plantarflexed or dorsiflexed first ray — transfers load laterally, producing transfer metatarsalgia, second metatarsal stress fracture, and callus under the second and third metatarsal heads. The callus pattern on the sole is a load map; read it.

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
Why is the ankle spared primary arthritis despite the highest loads? Several anatomical reasons: ankle cartilage is thinner but stiffer and more resistant to degradation, the joint is highly congruent so load is evenly distributed, and it has a very tightly constrained motion arc.

The clinical corollary is important: ankle osteoarthritis in a patient without a history of trauma should prompt a search for a cause — previous occult fracture, chronic instability, inflammatory arthritis, haemochromatosis or haemophilia.

It also means that restoring the mortise anatomically after a fracture matters enormously. A 1 mm lateral shift of the talus reduces the tibiotalar contact area by around 40%, and that is the pathway to post-traumatic arthritis.

content_config.body:
• Plafond (pilon) — the horizontal articular roof of the mortise, concave anteroposteriorly.
  • Medial malleolus — the short medial wall, with two colliculi: the anterior colliculus (longer, giving attachment to the superficial deltoid) and the posterior colliculus (the deep deltoid attaches at the intercollicular groove and posterior colliculus).
  • Posterior malleolus — not a true malleolus but the posterior lip of the plafond. Fractures here affect stability when they involve more than roughly 25% of the articular surface, and they carry the PITFL.
  • Fibular (incisura) notch laterally — receives the fibula and houses the syndesmotic ligaments.

• The lateral malleolus extends about 1 cm more distally and lies more posteriorly than the medial malleolus.
  • It bears no significant axial load (the fibula carries only about 10–15% of leg load), but it is the lateral buttress of the mortise — its position determines talar position.
  • The peroneal tendons groove its posterior surface, retained by the superior peroneal retinaculum.

content_config.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content_config.text:
The fibula is the key to ankle fracture stability. Because the talus follows the fibula, a shortened or malrotated lateral malleolus displaces the talus laterally, and it is that talar shift — not the fracture line itself — that destroys the joint.

This is why fibular length and rotation are restored meticulously in surgery, and why you should look at the medial clear space on a mortise view: widening indicates talar shift and deltoid or syndesmotic disruption even when the medial malleolus is intact.

The Maisonneuve fracture is the trap: a proximal fibular fracture with a syndesmotic and deltoid injury, presenting as an apparently isolated medial ankle injury. Palpate the whole length of the fibula in every ankle injury with medial tenderness.

content_config.body:
• About 60% of its surface is articular cartilage, and it has no muscular or tendinous attachments whatsoever — unique among the major bones.
  • Three parts: body (the trochlea, in the mortise), neck (the only substantially non-articular part, where vessels enter), and head (articulating with the navicular).
  • Lateral process — fractured in forced dorsiflexion with inversion; the "snowboarder’s fracture", classically missed and mistaken for a sprain.
  • Posterior process — with medial and lateral tubercles, and the groove for flexor hallucis longus between them. An unfused lateral tubercle is the os trigonum (present in roughly 7–14%), the usual cause of posterior ankle impingement in dancers and footballers.

content_config.text: 2.3.2 Blood supply — the reason talar fractures are feared

rows: Artery of the tarsal canal (posterior tibial artery)
The dominant supply to the talar body
Artery of the tarsal sinus (perforating peroneal + lateral tarsal)
Medial body — often the last supply remaining

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
The talus is supplied largely in retrograde fashion, with vessels entering distally at the neck and running backwards into the body. A displaced talar neck fracture therefore devascularises the body, with AVN rates rising steeply with displacement — from around 10% in undisplaced fractures to 50–90% in fracture-dislocations (the Hawkins classification).

Hawkins sign is a piece of anatomy you can read off a radiograph: a subchondral lucency in the talar dome at 6–8 weeks indicates that revascularisation and disuse osteopenia are occurring, and therefore that the bone is alive. Its presence is reassuring; its absence suggests AVN.

The deltoid branches are why preserving the deltoid ligament is emphasised in talar surgery — they may be the only supply left.

content_config.body:
• The largest tarsal bone, and the one that takes the impact of heel strike.
  • Three facets articulate with the talus: the posterior facet (largest, the main subtalar articulation), and the middle and anterior facets, which sit anteriorly and share a joint capsule with the talonavicular joint.
  • Sustentaculum tali — a medial shelf supporting the talar neck. The flexor hallucis longus runs in a groove beneath it, and the spring ligament and deltoid attach to it. It usually stays attached to the talus in fractures (the "constant fragment").
  • Tarsal sinus and canal — the funnel-shaped space between the posterior and middle facets, containing the interosseous talocalcaneal and cervical ligaments and the artery of the tarsal sinus.
  • Insertions: Achilles posteriorly; plantar fascia and the intrinsic muscles from the medial process of the tuberosity.
  • Böhler’s angle 20–40° and the critical angle of Gissane 120–145° — flattening of Böhler’s angle indicates a depressed intra-articular fracture.

• Navicular — the keystone of the medial arch, sitting between the talar head and the three cuneiforms. Its tuberosity receives the main tibialis posterior insertion. It has a relatively avascular central third, which is why navicular stress fractures (classically in sprinters and jumpers) heal poorly and are a genuine cause of delayed diagnosis.
  • An accessory navicular is present in about 10–15% of people. It is a common cause of medial midfoot pain in adolescents and is associated with tibialis posterior dysfunction, because the tendon inserts into the accessory ossicle rather than onto the navicular proper.
  • Cuboid — the lateral counterpart. The peroneus longus tendon grooves its plantar surface before crossing the sole. Cuboid syndrome (a subtle subluxation) is a recognised though contested cause of persistent lateral midfoot pain after an inversion injury.
  • Three cuneiforms — wedge-shaped, forming the transverse arch, with the intermediate cuneiform as its keystone. The intermediate cuneiform is recessed proximally, creating the bony mortise that receives the second metatarsal base.

• First metatarsal — short, broad and strong; carries about twice the load of any lesser ray. Its head bears the two sesamoids on its plantar surface.
  • Second metatarsal — the longest and most rigidly fixed, because its base is recessed into the cuneiform mortise. That rigidity makes it the classic site of stress fracture ("march fracture").
  • Fifth metatarsal — three clinically distinct fracture zones, and they behave very differently:
  • — Zone 1, the tuberosity — avulsion by the peroneus brevis (and the lateral plantar fascia band). The "pseudo-Jones" fracture. Heals well; symptomatic treatment.
  • — Zone 2, the metaphyseal–diaphyseal junction — the true Jones fracture, in a vascular watershed. Slow union, high non-union rate; often fixed in athletes.
  • — Zone 3, the proximal diaphysis — a stress fracture; also poor healing.

• Two sesamoids lie beneath the first metatarsal head, embedded within the tendons of flexor hallucis brevis and held by the intersesamoid ligament; the FHL tendon runs between them.
  • They increase the moment arm of the hallux flexors and absorb load beneath the first metatarsal head.
  • The medial (tibial) sesamoid is larger, bears more load and is more often injured. A bipartite medial sesamoid occurs in about 10% and is usually bilateral — do not call it a fracture without comparing sides.

• The hallux has two phalanges; the lesser toes have three.
  • Each metatarsophalangeal joint has a plantar plate — a thick fibrocartilaginous structure continuous with the plantar fascia and the collateral ligaments. Plantar plate rupture (commonly the second MTP) produces a dorsally subluxing, drifting toe and is a frequently missed cause of metatarsalgia.

content_config.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content_config.text: Turf toe is a hyperextension injury of the first MTP plantar plate and capsule, not a sprain of the joint in general. It matters because the plantar plate and sesamoid complex are what anchor the windlass; disrupting them impairs push-off long-term. It needs protection and stiff-soled footwear, not early return to sport.

content_config.body:
• A hinge (ginglymus), but with an oblique axis running roughly through the tips of the two malleoli.
  • Because the lateral malleolus is more distal and posterior, the axis is externally rotated about 20–30° relative to the knee axis and declined about 10° from horizontal.
  • Consequence: dorsiflexion is coupled with slight abduction and pronation; plantarflexion with adduction and supination. There is no such thing as pure sagittal ankle motion.
  • Close-packed position: full dorsiflexion. Loose-packed: about 10° plantarflexion, midway between inversion and eversion.

• Formed by three facets, but functionally one triplanar joint with an oblique axis running roughly 42° from the horizontal and 16–23° from the sagittal midline.
  • Because the axis is oblique, motion is triplanar and coupled:
  • — Supination = inversion + adduction + plantarflexion
  • — Pronation = eversion + abduction + dorsiflexion
  • In closed chain (foot on the ground), the same motions appear as rotation of the tibia: pronation drives internal tibial rotation, supination drives external rotation.

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
The subtalar joint is the torque converter between the foot and the leg. It transforms rotation of the leg into inversion and eversion of the foot, and vice versa.

That coupling is why foot posture influences the knee and hip. Excessive or prolonged pronation drives internal tibial and femoral rotation, which increases the dynamic Q angle and is one mechanism linking foot mechanics to patellofemoral pain. It is also why orthoses can influence symptoms well above the foot.

It also explains why subtalar motion must be assessed separately from ankle motion. A patient can have a stiff, arthritic subtalar joint with a perfectly mobile ankle — and they will struggle specifically on uneven ground, because that is the joint’s job.

content_config.body:
• A fibrous joint (syndesmosis), not synovial — though a small synovial recess from the ankle extends into it.
  • It permits only a few degrees of motion, but that motion is essential: in dorsiflexion the fibula moves laterally about 1 mm, rotates externally and translates proximally to accommodate the wider anterior talus.
  • Four ligaments hold it (see 4.3).

• Mechanism: external rotation of the foot with the ankle dorsiflexed — the wide talus is driven between the malleoli and levers them apart.
  • Clinical: pain above the joint line, over the anterolateral tibiofibular region; pain on the squeeze test and the external rotation stress test; pain reproduced by dorsiflexion rather than plantarflexion.
  • It matters because recovery is roughly twice as long as a lateral sprain — often 6–12 weeks rather than 2–4 — and frank diastasis requires fixation. Misdiagnosing it as a routine sprain leads to premature return and persistent symptoms.

• The talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joints, forming an S-shaped line across the foot with two axes (longitudinal and oblique).
  • The locking mechanism is the key concept: when the subtalar joint is supinated, the two midtarsal axes become non-parallel and the midfoot locks into a rigid lever. When the subtalar joint is pronated, the axes become parallel and the midfoot unlocks into a flexible, shock-absorbing structure.

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
This is the anatomical basis of normal gait. At heel strike the subtalar joint pronates, the midfoot unlocks and the foot becomes a flexible shock absorber that adapts to the ground. Through midstance into push-off, the subtalar joint supinates, the midfoot locks, and the foot becomes a rigid lever for propulsion.

A foot that fails to re-supinate — as in posterior tibial tendon dysfunction — stays unlocked at push-off and must propel from a flexible structure. That is inefficient, painful, and progressively deforming.

content_config.body:
• The junction between midfoot and forefoot, comprising three columns:
  • — Medial column: first metatarsal and medial cuneiform — some mobility.
  • — Middle column: second and third metatarsals with their cuneiforms — essentially rigid.
  • — Lateral column: fourth and fifth metatarsals with the cuboid — the most mobile, allowing the lateral foot to adapt to uneven ground.
  • The second metatarsal base is recessed into a mortise between the medial and lateral cuneiforms — the keystone of a transverse Roman-arch construction.
  • There is no ligament between the first and second metatarsal bases. The only restraint is the Lisfranc ligament, running obliquely from the medial cuneiform to the plantar base of the second metatarsal.

content_config.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content_config.text:
The Lisfranc injury is one of the most commonly missed injuries in the body — reportedly in 20–40% of cases — and it does badly when missed, progressing to midfoot collapse and arthritis.

The clues: midfoot swelling out of proportion to the history, plantar ecchymosis at the arch (highly suggestive), inability to bear weight, and pain on passive pronation–abduction of the forefoot.

Non-weight-bearing radiographs are frequently normal. Obtain weight-bearing views of both feet and look for widening between the first and second metatarsal bases, or a "fleck sign" (a small avulsion in that interval). If suspicion persists, get CT.

content_config.body:
• The MTP joints are condyloid, permitting flexion, extension and a little abduction/adduction.
  • Each has a plantar plate, collateral ligaments (taut in flexion) and a capsule; the deep transverse metatarsal ligament links the plates.
  • The hallux MTP requires about 65° of dorsiflexion for normal push-off. Less than this is hallux limitus; a stiff, arthritic joint is hallux rigidus.

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
Hallux MTP dorsiflexion is the gateway to the windlass mechanism (see 4.5). If the hallux cannot extend, the plantar fascia cannot wind around the metatarsal head, the arch cannot rise, and the foot cannot lock for push-off.

The patient compensates by rolling off the lateral border of the foot or by early heel rise — which produces lateral forefoot callus, transfer metatarsalgia and, over time, symptoms further up the chain. Measure hallux dorsiflexion in every foot examination. It takes five seconds and explains a great deal.

rows: Calcaneus, talus, navicular, three cuneiforms, metatarsals 1–3
High and mobile — the shock absorber. Where most pathology occurs
Low and rigid — built to transmit load directly to the ground
Cuboid and the three cuneiforms; the metatarsal bases
A true Roman arch; supported by muscular slings

content_config.body: • The transverse arch is slung by the peroneus longus laterally and tibialis posterior medially, whose tendons cross beneath the foot in opposite directions, plus the transverse head of adductor hallucis distally.

content_config.text: 4.2 The four layers of arch support

content_config.body: Support is layered, and the layers fail in order. Knowing the order tells you what stage a flatfoot has reached.

• Bone shape and joint congruity — the passive skeletal architecture. Contributes least.
  • Plantar ligaments — in order of contribution: the plantar fascia (providing roughly 25% of arch stiffness on its own), then the long plantar, short plantar and spring (calcaneonavicular) ligaments. This is the main static support.
  • Extrinsic muscles — tibialis posterior above all, with peroneus longus, FHL and FDL. The main dynamic support.
  • Intrinsic muscles — the "core" of the foot. Long underestimated; now recognised as important stabilisers, particularly under fatigue and in single-leg loading.

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
Arches are not held up by muscles alone. In quiet standing, EMG shows very little intrinsic or extrinsic muscle activity — the arch is held by ligament and bone. Muscles become important dynamically, during gait, and under load.

That has two practical consequences. First, "strengthening the arch" will not correct a ligamentous flatfoot at rest — but intrinsic foot training does improve dynamic control and is worth doing. Second, once the spring ligament and plantar fascia have failed, the deformity becomes structural, and no amount of muscle work will restore the arch.

content_config.body: Described by Hicks in 1954, and probably the single most useful biomechanical concept in the foot.

• The plantar fascia runs from the medial calcaneal tuberosity forward, dividing into five slips that insert into the plantar plates and proximal phalanges of the toes.
  • It therefore passes beneath the metatarsal heads and attaches distal to the MTP joints.
  • At push-off, the MTP joints dorsiflex — the toes extend as the heel rises. The fascia is wound around the metatarsal head like a cable around a drum.
  • Winding shortens the distance between the calcaneus and the metatarsal heads, which:
  • — raises the medial longitudinal arch,
  • — inverts the hindfoot,
  • — locks the midtarsal joint,
  • — and externally rotates the tibia through the subtalar coupling.
  • The result is an automatic, passive conversion of the foot into a rigid lever — achieved with no muscular effort at all.

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
The windlass explains a whole family of clinical problems.

Hallux rigidus or limitus blocks the windlass at source → no arch rise, no locking, compensatory lateral roll-off.

Plantar fasciitis is loading pathology at the proximal attachment, which is why the windlass test (passive hallux dorsiflexion reproducing heel pain) supports the diagnosis, and why first-step pain in the morning occurs — the fascia has shortened overnight and is abruptly loaded.

Plantar fascia release predictably lowers the arch and reduces push-off power, because the windlass cable has been cut. This is why complete release has fallen out of favour.

A rigid, high-arched (cavus) foot has an over-tight windlass — poor shock absorption, high plantar pressures, and lateral overload.

content_config.body:
• Flexible — the arch is absent on standing but restores on tiptoe or on passive hallux dorsiflexion (Jack’s test), confirming an intact windlass. Common, often asymptomatic, and treated only if symptomatic.
  • Rigid — the arch does not restore. Always abnormal. In an adolescent, think tarsal coalition; in an adult, think advanced posterior tibial dysfunction, arthritis or Charcot.
  • Tarsal coalition — a congenital bar between tarsal bones, most often talocalcaneal or calcaneonavicular. Presents in adolescence as a rigid flatfoot with peroneal spasm and recurrent "sprains". CT or MRI is diagnostic.

• A high, rigid arch with clawed toes and often a varus hindfoot.
  • Poor shock absorption, small contact area, high focal plantar pressures, and lateral column overload — hence recurrent ankle sprains, fifth metatarsal fractures and lateral foot pain.

content_config.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content_config.text:
A cavus foot demands a neurological explanation until you have excluded one. Roughly two-thirds of pes cavus is neurogenic, most commonly Charcot–Marie–Tooth disease, but also spinal dysraphism, tethered cord, Friedreich ataxia and old poliomyelitis.

Examine and ask accordingly: family history, clawing, intrinsic wasting, weak evertors with relatively preserved invertors, absent ankle jerks, and any spinal cutaneous stigmata. A unilateral or rapidly progressive cavus foot warrants spinal imaging.

The Coleman block test determines whether the hindfoot varus is driven by a plantarflexed first ray (flexible) or is fixed — which decides whether orthotic management can work.

content_config.body: Three ligaments, and they fail in a predictable order. Learn them from anterior to posterior, because that is the sequence of injury.

rows: Anterior lateral malleolus → talar neck. The weakest, and a thickening of the capsule rather than a discrete band
Injured in ~70% of ankle sprains — the first to fail. Tested by the anterior drawer
Tip of lateral malleolus → lateral calcaneus, deep to the peroneal tendons. Crosses BOTH the ankle and subtalar joints
Injured second, usually with the ATFL (~20% of sprains). Tested by talar tilt
Rarely injured in isolation — its rupture implies a severe injury or a dislocation

content_config.label: Memory aid
content_config.text:
"A-C-P" from anterior to posterior, and that is also the order of failure and of increasing strength. ATFL is weakest and first; PTFL is strongest and last.

And the reciprocal taut positions: ATFL is taut in plantarflexion, CFL in dorsiflexion. So test the ATFL with the ankle slightly plantarflexed and the CFL with it in neutral or dorsiflexion — otherwise you will get a false negative.

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
Why the CFL matters more than its injury rate suggests. It is the only lateral ligament crossing both the talocrural and subtalar joints. Its disruption therefore produces combined ankle and subtalar instability, which is harder to rehabilitate and more likely to become chronic.

It also runs deep to the peroneal tendons, so a CFL injury commonly involves the peroneal sheath — one reason lateral ankle pain persists after the ligament has healed.

Chronic ankle instability is as much neurological as mechanical. The lateral ligaments are richly supplied with mechanoreceptors, and injury impairs proprioception and peroneal reflex latency. This is why balance and proprioceptive training outperforms bracing and strengthening alone, and why it is the single best-evidenced intervention for preventing recurrent sprains.

content_config.body: • A strong triangular complex with superficial and deep layers. It is far stronger than the lateral complex — which is why medial injuries are less common but more significant.

rows: Tibionavicular · tibiospring · tibiocalcaneal · superficial posterior tibiotalar. Crosses both ankle and subtalar joints
Resists eversion and hindfoot valgus; blends with and supports the spring ligament
Anterior and posterior tibiotalar ligaments, running from the intercollicular groove to the talus. Short, thick, intra-articular
The primary restraint to lateral talar translation and external rotation — the true stabiliser of the mortise medially

content_config.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content_config.text:
Medial tenderness in an ankle fracture is a stability question, not a comfort question. Deltoid rupture allows the talus to translate laterally, converting a stable fibular fracture into an unstable one.

So in any ankle injury: palpate medially, look for medial clear space widening on the mortise view, and palpate the entire fibula to exclude a Maisonneuve injury. An isolated distal fibular fracture with medial tenderness is unstable until proven otherwise.

The deep deltoid also carries arterial branches to the talar body — another reason it is preserved surgically.

rows: The distal continuation of the interosseous membrane. The principal stabiliser
The first to fail in external rotation injury. Its distal fascicle (Bassett’s ligament) can impinge on the talus after injury and cause persistent anterolateral pain
Stronger than the AITFL; avulsed with posterior malleolar fractures
The deep component of the PITFL; acts as a labrum, deepening the posterior mortise

content_config.text: 5.4 The spring ligament and the medial arch

content_config.body:
• The plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament runs from the sustentaculum tali to the navicular, forming a sling beneath the talar head.
  • It has superomedial (the stronger, fibrocartilaginous part, which the talar head rests on) and inferoplantar components, and blends with the superficial deltoid.
  • It is the static keystone of the medial longitudinal arch; the tibialis posterior tendon is its dynamic partner.

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
Static and dynamic support fail together. Tibialis posterior dysfunction increases load on the spring ligament; the spring ligament stretches; the talar head drops medially and plantarward; the arch collapses. Once the spring ligament has failed, the deformity becomes structural rather than functional — which is the transition from a correctable to a fixed flatfoot, and the point at which orthoses and tendon work stop being sufficient.

This is why the examination question "is the hindfoot valgus correctable?" matters more than any imaging finding in progressive collapsing foot deformity.

content_config.body:
• A thick fibrous sheet from the medial calcaneal tuberosity to the forefoot, with medial, central and lateral bands. The central band is the thickest and the one that matters clinically.
  • Distally it divides into five slips, each inserting into a plantar plate and the base of a proximal phalanx — which is what makes the windlass possible.
  • It contributes about 25% of the stiffness of the medial arch, more than any other single structure.
  • Plantar fasciitis is a misnomer — histology shows degenerative change with little inflammation, so plantar fasciopathy or plantar heel pain is preferable. Pain is at the medial calcaneal tuberosity, classically worst on the first steps after rest.
  • Associated with limited ankle dorsiflexion, obesity, prolonged standing, and a sudden increase in load. Limited dorsiflexion is the most consistently modifiable risk factor — which is why calf stretching and load management form the core of treatment.

• Interosseous talocalcaneal ligament and cervical ligament — in the tarsal canal and sinus. Primary restraints to excessive subtalar motion; they also carry proprioceptive fibres, and are implicated in sinus tarsi syndrome after inversion injury.
  • Bifurcate ligament — calcaneonavicular and calcaneocuboid limbs, from the anterior calcaneus. Avulsed at the anterior process of the calcaneus in inversion injuries, a commonly missed fracture that mimics a lateral sprain.
  • Long and short plantar ligaments — support the lateral arch; the long plantar ligament forms the tunnel for peroneus longus over the cuboid.
  • Lisfranc ligament — from the medial cuneiform to the base of the second metatarsal, which is recessed into a bony mortise. There is no ligament between the first and second metatarsal bases, so the Lisfranc ligament is the sole restraint. Widening between the first and second metatarsal bases on a weight-bearing film is the diagnostic sign of an injury that is frequently missed and does badly when it is.
Everything crossing the ankle passes through one of four retinacular compartments. Learn the contents of each and you can localise almost any ankle symptom by position alone.

rows: Tibialis anterior · Extensor hallucis longus · Anterior tibial artery · Deep peroneal nerve · Extensor digitorum longus · peroneus tertius
Tibialis posterior · flexor Digitorum longus · posterior tibial Artery · tibial Nerve · flexor Hallucis longus

content_config.label: Memory aid
content_config.text:
Tarsal tunnel, front to back: "Tom, Dick, And a Very Nervous Harry" — Tibialis posterior, flexor Digitorum longus, Artery, Vein, Nerve (tibial), flexor Hallucis longus.

Anterior compartment, medial to lateral: "The Hospital Ain’t Doing Everything Properly" — Tibialis anterior, extensor Hallucis longus, Artery, Deep peroneal nerve, Extensor digitorum longus, Peroneus tertius.

And a positional rule: peroneus Brevis is Bone-side — it lies directly against the fibula, deep to peroneus longus. That is why brevis is the tendon that splits in longitudinal tears.

cells: Gastrocnemius: medial and lateral femoral condyles (so it crosses the knee). Soleus: posterior tibia and fibula, soleal line
Middle third of the posterior calcaneal tuberosity, with the retrocalcaneal bursa deep to it and the subcutaneous bursa superficial
Tibial nerve (S1, S2) — the ankle jerk tests S1
Plantarflexion and propulsion; gastrocnemius also flexes the knee. Generates the largest forces of any tendon in the body — up to 10–12 × body weight in running

The fibres spiral roughly 90° as they descend, which stores elastic energy but concentrates stress. There is a hypovascular watershed zone 2–6 cm above the insertion — the site of most midportion tendinopathy and most ruptures. It has no true synovial sheath, only a paratenon, so "tenosynovitis" here is really paratendinopathy

content_config.body:
• Insertional tendinopathy is a distinct entity at the calcaneal insertion, often with a retrocalcaneal bursitis and a Haglund deformity (a prominent posterosuperior calcaneal tuberosity).
  • Rupture is usually 2–6 cm above the insertion, in the watershed zone, and the Simmonds–Thompson test (absent plantarflexion on calf squeeze with the patient prone) is the key examination finding.

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
The distinction between midportion and insertional tendinopathy changes the treatment, and it is purely anatomical.

Midportion (2–6 cm above the insertion) responds well to full-range eccentric loading, including dropping the heel below the step.

Insertional tendinopathy is made worse by that same exercise, because dorsiflexion beyond neutral compresses the tendon against the calcaneus and the retrocalcaneal bursa. Load it in a restricted range, avoiding end-range dorsiflexion, and often with a small heel raise.

Getting this wrong is one of the commonest reasons Achilles rehabilitation fails. Palpate the exact level of tenderness before prescribing.

cells: Interosseous membrane and the adjacent posterior tibia and fibula — the deepest muscle of the posterior compartment
Principally the navicular tuberosity, with expansions to all three cuneiforms, the cuboid and the bases of metatarsals 2–4

The principal invertor and a plantarflexor. Critically, it supinates the subtalar joint at push-off, locking the midfoot and converting the foot into a rigid lever. It is the main dynamic support of the medial longitudinal arch

It has its own hypovascular zone just distal and posterior to the medial malleolus, where it changes direction — the site of degeneration in posterior tibial tendon dysfunction (progressive collapsing foot deformity). Because its lever arm for inversion is short, even mild dysfunction produces disproportionate deformity

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
Two bedside tests, both derived directly from the anatomy:

The "too many toes" sign — viewed from behind, more toes are visible lateral to the leg on the affected side, because the forefoot has abducted at the midtarsal joint as the arch collapsed.

The single-leg heel raise — the most useful test. To rise onto the toes, the subtalar joint must supinate and the midfoot must lock, and tibialis posterior initiates that. A patient who cannot perform a single heel raise, or whose heel fails to swing into varus when they do, has tibialis posterior dysfunction. Test it before the deformity is fixed — that is when treatment works.

rows: Crosses the sole beneath the cuboid → base of the 1st metatarsal and medial cuneiform
Everts and plantarflexes the first ray, so it stabilises the medial column at push-off and helps maintain the transverse arch
The primary evertor. Its insertion is avulsed in the pseudo-Jones fracture. Lying against the fibula, it is the tendon that splits longitudinally

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
The peroneals are the dynamic defence against inversion injury. After a lateral sprain, peroneal reaction time is prolonged — which is a large part of why sprains recur. Peroneal strengthening plus balance training is therefore not generic rehabilitation but a targeted mechanical intervention.

Persistent lateral ankle pain after a "sprain" should prompt three questions: is there a peroneal tendon tear (particularly a brevis split), is there peroneal subluxation from a torn superior peroneal retinaculum, and is there an anterior process of calcaneus or lateral talar process fracture? All three are commonly missed and all three are visible on ultrasound or CT.

content_config.body:
• Runs in a groove between the medial and lateral tubercles of the posterior talus, then beneath the sustentaculum tali — an acutely angled path through two fibro-osseous tunnels.
  • It is the most posterior and lateral structure in the tarsal tunnel, and crosses the sole to the distal phalanx of the hallux, passing between the two sesamoids.
  • It is the final push-off muscle, and a major dynamic supporter of the medial arch.
  • FHL tenosynovitis is the "dancer’s tendinitis", presenting with posteromedial ankle pain on rising onto demi-pointe, and frequently coexisting with posterior impingement from an os trigonum, since the two structures are immediate neighbours.
Twelve muscles cross from the leg into the foot. Group them by compartment and their nerve supply follows automatically.

rows: Tibialis anterior, EHL, EDL, peroneus tertius
Dorsiflexion, toe extension; tibialis anterior also inverts
Eversion; longus plantarflexes the first ray

content_config.label: Memory aid
content_config.text: Two muscles invert (both "tibialis"), two evert (both "peroneus"). Then just ask which side of the malleolus each passes: tibialis anterior passes in front of the medial malleolus (so it dorsiflexes and inverts), tibialis posterior behind it (plantarflexes and inverts). The peroneals pass behind the lateral malleolus (plantarflex and evert), except peroneus tertius, which passes in front and therefore dorsiflexes.

content_config.body: Twenty small muscles within the foot itself. Learn the plantar ones as four layers, superficial to deep — that is how they are dissected, imaged and injected.

rows: Quadratus plantae · four lumbricals; the FDL and FHL tendons pass through this layer
Lateral plantar (QP; lumbricals 2–4); medial plantar (1st lumbrical)
Flexor hallucis brevis (containing the sesamoids) · adductor hallucis (oblique and transverse heads) · flexor digiti minimi brevis
Medial plantar (FHB); lateral plantar (adductor hallucis, FDMB)
Three plantar interossei (adduct) · four dorsal interossei (abduct); the tibialis posterior and peroneus longus tendons cross here

content_config.label: Memory aid
content_config.text:
Layer 1 = two abductors with a flexor between them: Abductor hallucis, Flexor Digitorum Brevis, Abductor digiti minimi — medial, central, lateral.

PAD and DAB apply, as in the hand: Plantar interossei ADduct, Dorsal interossei ABduct. There are three plantar and four dorsal, and the reference axis is the second toe.

Quadratus plantae exists to fix an angle problem: FDL enters the foot obliquely from the medial side, so quadratus plantae pulls its tendon straight, allowing the toes to flex in line rather than deviating medially.

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
Almost all intrinsics are supplied by the tibial nerve via its plantar branches, and the only intrinsic supplied by the deep peroneal nerve is extensor digitorum brevis (plus EHB). That single exception makes EDB a useful needle target in peroneal neuropathy, and its visible wasting on the dorsolateral foot is an easy clinical sign.

Intrinsic wasting is an early and important sign of peripheral neuropathy. As the intrinsics fail, the long extensors and flexors act unopposed at the MTP joints, producing clawing — which drives the metatarsal heads plantarward, increases plantar pressure and generates ulcers in the diabetic foot. Clawed toes plus a high-arched appearance in a neuropathic patient is a pressure warning, not a cosmetic finding.

content_config.body:
• The foot has nine osteofascial compartments: medial, lateral, superficial central, deep central (calcaneal), four interosseous and the adductor compartment.
  • The calcaneal compartment contains quadratus plantae and communicates with the deep posterior compartment of the leg.

content_config.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content_config.text:
Foot compartment syndrome is a real and under-recognised entity, most often after calcaneal fractures, Lisfranc injuries or crush injury.

The cardinal sign is pain out of proportion, worsened by passive toe extension, with a tense, swollen foot. Pulses and capillary refill are usually normal — do not use them to exclude it.

Untreated, ischaemic contracture of quadratus plantae and the intrinsics produces fixed claw toes, a stiff painful foot and chronic plantar pressure problems. It is one of the more preventable causes of permanent foot disability.
7.1 The five nerves crossing the ankle

content_config.label: Memory aid
content_config.text: The dorsum of the foot is superficial peroneal territory, except the first web space, which is deep peroneal. That small patch is disproportionately useful — it is the only cutaneous territory of the deep peroneal nerve, so numbness confined to it localises precisely.
7.2 The tarsal tunnel and the plantar nerves

content_config.body:
• A fibro-osseous tunnel behind the medial malleolus, roofed by the flexor retinaculum (laciniate ligament) and floored by the talus, sustentaculum tali and calcaneus.
  • The tibial nerve divides within or just distal to the tunnel into three branches:
  • — Medial plantar nerve — the sole of the medial three and a half toes (the "median nerve of the foot").
  • — Lateral plantar nerve — the sole of the lateral one and a half toes.
  • — Medial calcaneal branches — arising proximally, often above the retinaculum, supplying the skin of the heel.
  • The first branch of the lateral plantar nerve (Baxter’s nerve) turns laterally between abductor hallucis and quadratus plantae to supply abductor digiti minimi.

content_config.label: EMG / electrodiagnostics
content_config.text:
Two anatomical facts localise heel pain.

The medial calcaneal branches usually arise proximal to the flexor retinaculum, so they are typically spared in tarsal tunnel syndrome. A patient with tarsal tunnel syndrome usually has numbness of the sole but a normal heel; numbness including the heel points more proximally.

Baxter’s neuropathy is entrapment of the first branch of the lateral plantar nerve between abductor hallucis and the medial calcaneal tuberosity. It causes chronic heel pain indistinguishable from plantar fasciitis but is worse with activity rather than on the first steps in the morning, and may show denervation of abductor digiti minimi on EMG. It accounts for a meaningful minority of recalcitrant heel pain.

Tarsal tunnel syndrome is over-diagnosed. Confirm it: sensory studies of the medial and lateral plantar nerves, mixed nerve studies, and needle examination of the intrinsics. Then look for a cause — unlike carpal tunnel syndrome, tarsal tunnel syndrome is usually secondary to a ganglion, varicosities, an accessory muscle, a space-occupying lesion, tenosynovitis or hindfoot valgus, and imaging finds a lesion in a substantial proportion of true cases.

content_config.body:
• Not a true neuroma — it is perineural fibrosis of a common plantar digital nerve.
  • Commonest in the third webspace, for two anatomical reasons: it is where the medial and lateral plantar nerve branches converge, making the nerve thicker, and it sits at the junction between the relatively fixed medial column and the mobile lateral column.
  • The nerve is compressed against the deep transverse metatarsal ligament during dorsiflexion of the toes.
  • Clinical: burning or electric forefoot pain radiating into the toes, relieved by removing the shoe and rubbing the foot; Mulder’s click on mediolateral compression with simultaneous plantar pressure.
  • Ultrasound shows a hypoechoic mass at the intermetatarsal space and guides injection.

• Joplin’s neuroma — the medial plantar digital nerve of the hallux, compressed by footwear or a bunion.
  • Deep peroneal nerve (anterior tarsal tunnel syndrome) — under the inferior extensor retinaculum; causes first-webspace numbness and may show EDB denervation. Tight laces and dorsal osteophytes are typical causes.
  • Superficial peroneal nerve — at the point where it pierces the deep fascia 10–12 cm above the lateral malleolus; produces dorsal foot numbness with no motor deficit, and is a recognised cause of persistent symptoms after an inversion sprain.

• Anterior tibial artery → becomes the dorsalis pedis at the ankle, running between the tendons of EHL and EDL — palpate it lateral to the EHL tendon. Absent in roughly 2–12% of normal people, so its absence alone is not diagnostic.
  • Posterior tibial artery → passes through the tarsal tunnel between FDL and FHL, dividing into the medial and lateral plantar arteries. Palpate it midway between the medial malleolus and the Achilles.
  • Peroneal artery → supplies the lateral compartment and contributes the perforating branch to the ankle and the artery of the tarsal sinus.
  • In the sole, the lateral plantar artery forms the deep plantar arch, completed medially by the deep plantar branch of the dorsalis pedis — the foot’s equivalent of the palmar arches.
  • A malleolar and calcaneal anastomotic network surrounds the ankle.

content_config.label: PM&R clinical pearl
content_config.text:
Palpating both the dorsalis pedis and the posterior tibial pulse is part of every ankle and foot examination, and mandatory before any injection, immobilisation or surgical referral. The distal limb is where vascular disease presents first.

In a diabetic patient, add sensory testing with a 10 g monofilament and inspection of the plantar surface and interdigital spaces. Neuropathic patients present late and present atypically — a warm, swollen, red foot with a normal or minimally painful history is a Charcot neuroarthropathy until proven otherwise, not cellulitis or a sprain. Missing it results in permanent midfoot collapse.

content_config.body: • Applying Hilton’s law, the ankle joint receives articular branches from the nerves of the muscles crossing it:

rows: Tibial nerve, with a contribution from the sural

content_config.body: • Practically, this multi-nerve supply is why a complete ankle block requires five injections — the two deep nerves (tibial and deep peroneal) plus the three subcutaneous ones (superficial peroneal, sural, saphenous).
Palpate systematically around the ankle in four zones, matching the four retinacular compartments.

• Lateral: tip and posterior edge of the lateral malleolus → ATFL (anteroinferior to the tip) → CFL (inferior to the tip) → peroneal tendons behind and below → base of the 5th metatarsal → anterior process of the calcaneus.
  • Medial: tip and posterior edge of the medial malleolus → deltoid ligament → tibialis posterior tendon (ask for resisted inversion to make it stand out) → navicular tuberosity → sustentaculum tali (about 1 finger-breadth below the medial malleolus).
  • Anterior: joint line with the ankle plantarflexed → tibialis anterior and EHL tendons → dorsalis pedis pulse lateral to EHL → anterolateral gutter.
  • Posterior: Achilles insertion, then the midportion 2–6 cm above it → retrocalcaneal space → posteromedial for FHL and the posterior tibial pulse.
  • Proximal: palpate the entire fibula to the head — for the Maisonneuve injury — and the syndesmosis above the joint line.
  • Then assess: dorsiflexion with the knee extended and flexed (Silfverskiöld), subtalar inversion and eversion, single-leg heel raise, and single-leg balance.

content_config.text: 8.1.1 The Ottawa ankle and foot rules

content_config.body:
• Radiograph the ankle if there is pain in the malleolar zone and any of: bone tenderness along the posterior edge or tip of the lateral malleolus (distal 6 cm), bone tenderness along the posterior edge or tip of the medial malleolus (distal 6 cm), or inability to bear weight for four steps both immediately and at assessment.
  • Radiograph the foot if there is midfoot pain and any of: tenderness at the base of the 5th metatarsal, tenderness over the navicular, or inability to bear weight as above.
  • Sensitivity approaches 98–100% for clinically significant fractures. They are validated in adults and in children over about 5 years.

content_config.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content_config.text:
The Ottawa rules exclude fracture, not injury. A negative rule does not exclude a syndesmotic injury, an osteochondral lesion of the talus, a peroneal tendon tear, a lateral talar process fracture or a Lisfranc injury — all of which are radiographically subtle or invisible.

Re-examine any "simple sprain" that has not substantially improved by 4–6 weeks, and consider imaging then.

content_config.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content_config.text: Do not inject corticosteroid into or around a weight-bearing tendon casually. The Achilles and tibialis posterior are the two where injection has been associated with rupture, and both are load-bearing structures whose failure is disabling. Load-based rehabilitation is first-line for both.
8.4 Common problems mapped back to anatomy

Mechanoreceptor damage → balance training outperforms bracing alone
External rotation in dorsiflexion levers the malleoli apart; recovery twice as long

content_config.body: This deserves its own section, because it is the foot problem a physiatrist is most likely to change the outcome of, and because it is driven entirely by anatomy.

• Sensory neuropathy removes the protective pain signal, so injury goes unnoticed. Assess with a 10 g monofilament at standard plantar sites; inability to feel it defines loss of protective sensation.
  • Motor neuropathy wastes the intrinsics first, so the long flexors and extensors act unopposed → claw toes, the metatarsal heads are driven plantarward, and the protective plantar fat pad migrates distally. Peak plantar pressure rises exactly where it is least protected.
  • Autonomic neuropathy produces dry, fissured skin and arteriovenous shunting — a warm foot that is nonetheless poorly perfused at tissue level.
  • The result is a predictable ulcer map: beneath the metatarsal heads (especially first and second), the hallux pulp, the heel, and over dorsal PIP joints of clawed toes from footwear.

content_config.label: Pitfall — do not miss
content_config.text:
Charcot neuroarthropathy is the diagnosis not to miss. A warm, swollen, erythematous foot in a neuropathic patient, often with minimal or no pain and frequently no fever or systemic upset. It is regularly misdiagnosed as cellulitis, gout or a sprain.

A temperature difference of more than about 2°C between feet in a neuropathic patient is a red flag. Early radiographs are often normal — do not wait for them.

Untreated, it produces midfoot collapse into a rocker-bottom deformity, and the resulting bony prominence ulcerates. Immediate offloading in a total contact cast while the diagnosis is being confirmed is far safer than waiting.

content_config.body:
• The talus is wider anteriorly — dorsiflexion is stable, plantarflexion is not. That is why sprains happen when they do.
  • Ten degrees of dorsiflexion is the functional threshold. Below it, the foot, knee and hip all compensate.
  • Use the Silfverskiöld test to separate gastrocnemius tightness from a true joint restriction.
  • ATFL → CFL → PTFL is the order of injury and of increasing strength.
  • The CFL crosses both the ankle and subtalar joints — its injury produces combined instability.
  • Medial tenderness in an ankle fracture is a stability question. Palpate the whole fibula for a Maisonneuve injury.
  • The talus has no muscle attachments and a retrograde blood supply — hence AVN after neck fracture, and the value of Hawkins sign.
  • Tarsal tunnel, front to back: Tom, Dick, And a Very Nervous Harry.
  • Midportion Achilles tendinopathy loves full-range eccentric loading; insertional tendinopathy hates it — palpate the level first.
  • Tibialis posterior locks the midfoot at push-off. The single-leg heel raise is the test.
  • The subtalar joint converts leg rotation into foot inversion and eversion — the link between foot posture and the knee.
  • Chronic ankle instability is proprioceptive as much as mechanical. Balance training is the best-evidenced intervention.
  • The first dorsal web space is the only deep peroneal territory — numbness there localises precisely.
  • Ankle osteoarthritis without trauma needs a cause found.
  • A warm, swollen, minimally painful foot in a neuropathic patient is Charcot until proven otherwise.
  • The windlass converts the foot into a rigid lever passively — no muscle required. Hallux dorsiflexion is its switch.
  • Measure hallux MTP dorsiflexion in every foot examination. Below 65° the windlass fails and load transfers laterally.
  • Jack’s test and tiptoe standing separate a flexible from a rigid flatfoot. A rigid flatfoot is always abnormal — in adolescence, think tarsal coalition.
  • A cavus foot needs a neurological explanation — about two-thirds are neurogenic, most often Charcot–Marie–Tooth.
  • The second metatarsal is the longest and most rigid, hence the march fracture; the fifth has three fracture zones with very different prognoses.
  • Read the callus pattern on the sole — it is a load map.
  • Weight-bearing radiographs of both feet are what reveal a Lisfranc injury; non-weight-bearing films are frequently normal.
  • EDB is the only intrinsic supplied by the deep peroneal nerve — useful on EMG and visible on inspection.
  • Claw toes in a neuropathic foot are a pressure warning, not a cosmetic finding.

• Warm, swollen, erythematous foot in a patient with neuropathy → Charcot neuroarthropathy. Offload immediately; do not wait for radiographic change.
  • Inability to weight-bear with tenderness at the malleoli, navicular or base of the 5th metatarsal → apply the Ottawa rules and image.
  • Persistent lateral pain after a "sprain" → peroneal tendon tear or subluxation, lateral talar process fracture, anterior process fracture, or an osteochondral lesion.
  • Midfoot swelling with plantar bruising after a twisting injury → Lisfranc injury. Weight-bearing radiographs; it is missed in up to 20–40% of cases and does badly untreated.
  • Sudden posterior calf pain with a palpable gap and a positive Simmonds–Thompson test → Achilles rupture. Note that patients can often still weakly plantarflex using FHL and tibialis posterior, so do not exclude it because they can move the foot.
  • Progressive flatfoot with an inability to perform a single heel raise → posterior tibial dysfunction; treat before the deformity becomes fixed.
  • Pain out of proportion with a tense foot, worse on passive toe extension, after calcaneal or Lisfranc injury → foot compartment syndrome. Normal pulses do not exclude it.
  • Any ulcer in a neuropathic foot → probe to bone; a positive probe-to-bone test strongly suggests osteomyelitis.
  • Unilateral or rapidly progressive cavus foot with clawing → image the spine and investigate for a hereditary neuropathy.
  • Rest pain, absent pulses, or non-healing ulceration → vascular assessment before anything else.
Anatomy only. Gait analysis, orthotic prescription and surgical reconstruction are treated separately.
